content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper is about alleviating the over-smoothing issue of Graph Attention Networks (GATs). The background is that Graph Convolutional Networks (CGNs) and GATs are widely used architectures in graph neural networks (GNNs), and both suffer from over-smoothing issues. The authors claim that existing researches mainly focus on alleviating the issue for GCNs, and the proposed techniques cannot fit GATs well. In this work, the authors verify their hypothesis that the over-smoothing issue that happens in deep GATs is caused by the overwhelming propagation from nodes with large degrees as the number of layers increases. To alleviate the over-smoothing issue of GATs, they propose a simple and deep version of GAT named Layer-wise Self-Adaptive GAT (LSGAT), which adjusts the attention coefficients with the layer depth and regularizes the coefficients for nodes with a large degree. The authors verify the effectiveness of the proposed LSGAT empirically.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strong points: 
1. The authors demonstrate that overwhelming propagation from large-degree nodes may result in the over-smoothing issue on deep GATs. This finding is meaningful, 

2. The whole paper is generally of great readability and well-written. 

3. The authors perform extensive experiments to empirically verify the effectiveness of the proposed LSGAT by comparing it with existing methods. LSGAT is also effective when combined with other techniques.


Weakness:
1. The authors should present in what scenarios people should or should not use your method. The results in Figure 4 demonstrate that the proposed method achieves comparable performances with the established methods (e.g., DropEdge, DGN, and PairNorm) when setting two GNN layers, while outperforming all the methods when adopting 15 or 60 GNN layers. Considering that people usually use a few GNN layers in real-world applications to avoid node embeddings converging to similar vectors, I suggest the authors investigate the effectiveness of all the methods when setting 5 and 10 GNN layers. 

2. The final goal of solving the over-smoothing issue is having good prediction performance by using deep layers. Results in Figure 4 show that when adding more layers, the performance of all models, including LSGAT, will decrease. Then, in these specific scenarios, what is the point of adding more layers? By handling the over-smoothing issue, can the proposed model LSGAT outperforms all existing GNN models, in the classification task?

3. A few claims in the paper might not be strict. For example, “Their techniques cannot well fit the GATs models due to the inherent difference between these two architectures.” Some existing methods, e.g., DropEdge, can also be well-adopted to GATs to alleviate the over-smoothing issue. 

4. The authors should consider the intrinsic characteristics of the graph, thus being strict and avoiding misleading. The authors verify that the over-smoothing of GATs is closely related to the overwhelming propagation from large-degree nodes. The finding may not be thorough. Concretely, for graphs, in which those large-degree nodes are all embraced by the nodes from the same class, the proposed method, which regularizes attention coefficients for large-degree nodes, may hinder the message-passing process within the same class and become less effective. From this perspective, I suggest the authors consider graphs’ intrinsic characteristics in both experiments and writing.

5. All of the six datasets used in the experiments are academic networks. Five of them are citation networks. More types of real-world networks are needed, aiming to have more convincing experimental results.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper investigates that the common over-smoothing problem in the deep GAT model could be relieved by considering the overwhelming propagation caused by the nodes with large degree. And the authors further propose their strategy which is a coefficient computation mechanism for training GAT. Some experimental results show the effectiveness of the proposed method on several datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The strengths of this paper are as follows:
First, his paper focuses on a classical research problem for training graph attention networks, which is important to the community.
Second, the paper is clearly written and the proposed method is easy to understand.
Third, the experiments show the effectiveness of the proposed method especially when the layer of GNN is deep.

The weaknesses of this paper are as follows:
First, the main concern is about the technical novelty. I think the over-smoothing problem has been widely explored in the literature. The main difference between them and the proposed method is not well discussed. 
Second, the time complexity as well as the empirical efficiency of the proposed method is not well discussed in the main paper, since relatively complex techniques are proposed in the model.
Third, the necessary comparisons with more baselines for the over-smoothing problem are also missing, which I think can be introduced in the experiments. And the improvements upon the GAT-Lip are marginal, which raises my concerns about the effectiveness.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The clarity of this paper is good, considering its clear expressions, while the novelty and experiment are two of my biggest concerns. It would be good if the authors can address these concerns above in their rebuttal.
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, this paper focuses on an important problem and proposes an effective method to tackle this problem. The main concerns lie in the technical novelty and some experiment analyses. I recommend weak reject for this paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies how to make Graph Attention Networks (GATs) deep while maintaining the performance as shallow models. The authors claim the oversmoothing issue that happened in deep GATs is caused by the overwhelming propagation from larger degree nodes when the number of layers increases. Motivated by this finding, they propose a new version of GATs named LSGAT with two designs of network architectures considering both neighboring and non-adjacent nodes during the aggregation process. Experiments on five real-world datasets show the effectiveness of LSGAT over GAT-based baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

* The empirical observation on the overwhelming propagation problem in deep GATs with the designed two baselines Zero-GAT and Reciprocal-GAT is interesting.
* The paper is generally well-written and almost clear everywhere to follow under the current setting.

Weaknesses:
* The importance of making GATs deeper needs further clarification. From a practical perspective, as we expect from the conventional setting of deep learning on grid-structured data, the very deep architectures should have a breakthrough in performance in comparison with shallow ones. However, from the experimental results, it is not clear whether a deeper graph neural network with ceteris paribus performs better since almost all two-layer GNNs achieve the best or on-par performance across all datasets. It is also unclear if a user really needs to use deep GNNs in practice, and what would gain from deeper GATs over GCNs.

* From a theoretical perspective, the authors are encouraged to conduct some theoretical analysis to support the finding of the overwhelming propagation problem or other aspects. For example, do deeper GATs increase the expressiveness of GNNs in comparison with deeper GCNs while handling the overwhelming propagation problems?

* The chosen five benchmark datasets are known to be “small world” networks with low diameter, where one can reach any node from any other node in a few hops. As a result, the receptive field of just a few convolutional layers already covers the entire graph [1], so adding more layers might not help to reach remote nodes. To demonstrate the necessity of deeper GNNs, some other datasets might be more suitable.

* The comparison of deep GATs to deep GCNs seems missing and the layers of deep GATs are only set to 30 as the maximum, which is not deep enough in my opinion. Could the authors provide the results of the comparison between 64-layer GATs and 64-layer GCNs?

[1] The logical expressiveness of graph neural networks, ICLR 2020
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:  The necessarity of deeper GATs over GCNs needs further clarification from either practical or theoretical perspective.

Quality: The empirical observation is interesting but the experimental designs and selection of datasets could be improved.

Novelty: The idea of making GATs deeper is not very novel in my opinion as pointed out in Weaknesses.

Reproducibility: The reproducibility is good with detailed experimental settings and provided codes.
content.summary_of_the_review: The importance of the studied problem needs further clarification and the experimental analysis is not very fair and informative.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper identifies the reason for oversmoothing issue in the GAT model as the overwhelming propagation from nodes with large degrees. Based on GAT, LSGAT is proposed with more properly weighted attention coefficients.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1. Compared with the vanilla GAT, LSGAT is much better at relieving the oversmoothing issue, especially when the network becomes deeper.
2. Extensive experiments are conducted to compare LSGAT with many models and techniques of similar purpose. Additionally, an ablation study over the model’s hyperparameter for the proportion of the nodes to be regularized is performed.


Weaknesses:

1. Although LSGAT indeed suffers less from oversmoothing than GAT and GAT-Lip, its empirical performance is still not good enough. In particular, the accuracy decreases as the number of layers increases, as shown in Figure 1 and Table 1. 
2. A stronger result is shown in Table 2 with the hybrid model LSGAT-GCNII. As the model gets deeper, its accuracy increases. However, it seems that this good performance is primarily due to GCNII. Without GCNII, as mentioned in the point above, LSGAT is not able to boost performance as the depth increases.
3. Table 2 also shows that LSGAT-GCNII suffers from oversmoothing more than GCNII because its accuracy starts to drop when the depth is 32 in Cora and Citeseer, while GCNII does not have this issue. And its initial better performance than GCNII seems to benefit from the attention layer, which is known to be more expressive than the convolutional layer.
4. It would be great if the authors could explain more about why $\eta$ is chosen in this way, at least intuitively.
5. The authors mention that the layer-wise scaling scores based on the overlap degree could be smoother in terms of continuity. Is it only valid for the Pubmed dataset or in general? More elaboration on this statement is encouraged.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
1. The paper is well written. However, the problem setting seems to be not clear enough. In particular, it proposes to tackle the oversmoothing issue, but the term ‘oversmoothing’ is not explained explicitly in the main body.

2. The code for the proposed method is submitted/uploaded.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper identifies a source of oversmoothing in GNN; from there, a new model is proposed based on GAT. The idea is innovative, but the empirical performance can be improved.

content.title: Simple and Deep Graph Attention Networks
content.abstract: Graph Attention Networks (GATs) and Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNs) are two state-of-the-art architectures in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). It is well known that both models suffer from performance degradation when more GNN layers are stacked, and many works have been devoted to address this problem. We notice that main research efforts in the line focus on the GCN models, and their techniques cannot well fit the GATs models due to the inherent difference between these two architectures. In GATs, the attention mechanism ignores the overwhelming propagation from certain nodes as the number of layers increases. To sufficiently utilize the expressive power of GATs, we propose a new version of GAT named Layer-wise Self-adaptive GAT (LSGAT), which can effectively alleviate the oversmoothing issue in deep GATs. We redesign the attention coefficients computation mechanism adaptively adjusted by layer depth, which considers both immediate neighboring and non-adjacent nodes from a global view. The experimental evaluation confirms that LSGAT consistently achieves better results on node classification tasks over relevant counterparts.
